task: build a small playable game or mechanic in a game engine (Roblox Studio, Scratch, Unity, Godot, GDevelop, Construct): start a project, build or place the scene — terrain, platforms, sprites, objects — then give it behaviour by scripting or wiring events, set the rules and values that make it work (speed, gravity, score, spawn, win and lose conditions), PLAYTEST it by running the game, then tune those values against what happened when you played, and publish or export it; complete when the game is published, exported, or shown running as intended. Surface pinned: the editor session that produces one playable thing. The distinctive decision here is the playtest loop: unlike every other creative domain in this set, the maker runs the artifact to find out whether it is right, then goes back and changes a number. Capture that loop, including what they noticed while playing. Off-task: gameplay, let's-plays and reviews of finished games, asset-pack and marketplace showcases, engine or hardware comparisons, game-design theory with no editor on screen, and monetisation or publishing-business advice.

tree.label: Build and playtest a small game
tree.note: 1 first, and 1.5 to 1.8 whenever the editor gets in the way - Nfpn and rWUb open the panels before anything else. then 2 for each object the game needs, with 3 for the ones that must collide or hold still. 4 for the behaviour, in blocks, in a script file or in an event sheet. 5 when the numbers are first chosen. 6 as soon as there is anything to see, and again after almost every change - eleven of twelve run the game, and q7wl is the one that never does. 7 whenever 6 shows something wrong, and it goes back into 2, 3, 4 or 5 depending on what broke. 8 only in rWUb, which then runs 6 against the published game and comes back through 7 and 8.5.

questions.question: Which version of the Godot engine should you download?

questions.check: What version number does the installed build show, and is it the standard or the .NET one?
questions.say_example: You downloaded Godot <4.1.2>, the <.NET> build. A tutorial written for the standard build may not match it.

questions.question: Is Roblox Studio installed and open, ready for you to start the project?

questions.verify_form: The agent chose where the engine unpacked - check the path; you will be launching it from there every time.
questions.check: What folder path did the engine's archive get extracted into?

questions.question: Do you want to look through the example projects, or start from an empty one?

questions.question: Is the version that downloaded the same one the page advertised?
questions.why: The Godot homepage prominently featured version 4.2 for download, but the file actually downloaded and extracted was version 4.1.3.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The delegator loses the assurance that the intended version of the game engine is being used, which could cause unexpected compatibility issues.
questions.check: Does the version on the download page match the version of the file that came down?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide whether to build entirely from scratch or use a pre-made template that saves time on asset management.
questions.verify_form: The agent remixed a starter project or opened an empty one - check which the editor is on; a remix brings the series' costumes with it and also carries whatever else was in it.
questions.check: Is the project a remix of an existing published project, or a new empty one?
questions.say_example: Remixing brings in <12> costumes and <3> scripts from someone else's project. Start from that, or from empty?

questions.question: Is the engine's project list open, ready for a new project?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to personally verify the project's initial configuration, template, and storage location.
questions.check: Is Unity Hub showing the Projects tab with a New Project button, rather than still on an install or update screen?

questions.check: Does the project still show the default Scratch Cat sprite and starting backdrop with nothing custom added?

questions.question: What will you name the project?

questions.say_example: The folder <MyGame_final2> already has files in it. Saving here mixes this project in with whatever's already there.

questions.question: Which name, folder and cloud settings should the new project use?
questions.why: The project name and location determine where your files are stored locally, while the cloud and version control checkboxes dictate whether your project is synced online.

questions.why: This matters because the engine requires a dedicated folder to resolve the path error and a renderer choice that dictates platform compatibility, such as desktop-only for Forward+.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this setup means losing the chance to optimize the engine's underlying graphics backend for your specific game type and target audience.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose a renderer - check which; the mobile one is fast on simple 2D scenes and the desktop one is the only route to advanced 3D.

questions.question: Are the Unity Cloud and Version Control options left enabled in the new project dialog?
questions.why: Leaving Unity Cloud and Version Control checked by default ties the local project to Unity's online services, which have storage quotas and potential billing implications for larger projects.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to opt out of a cloud service ecosystem that they may not want or need, potentially avoiding future account limits or unexpected fees.
questions.check: Are the Unity Cloud and Version Control checkboxes still checked in the project creation dialog?
questions.say_example: Unity Cloud and Version Control are still checked. That ties this project to online storage with its own limits.

questions.question: Should you work in the 2D or 3D workspace for this game?
questions.why: Selecting the 2D mode from the top bar ensures you have the correct tools and perspective for placing flat sprites instead of 3D meshes.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the spatial familiarity of the engine's ribbon menu and the personal preference of arranging your own workspace layout.

questions.why: Creating specific folders like 'scripts' and 'scenes' in the FileSystem dock keeps assets structured and easy to locate as the game grows.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to establish a folder structure that matches your specific mental model or workflow preferences.

questions.why: The FileSystem dock shows the 'audio' folder accidentally nested inside the 'graphics' folder, which needs to be corrected to keep project assets organized.

questions.check: Does the FileSystem panel show the audio folder nested inside the graphics folder, rather than at the project root?

questions.verify_form: The agent deleted or kept the default costumes - check the list; keeping them leaves art you did not make in the project.

questions.verify_form: The agent deleted a temporary node - check the tree; anything left behind still draws and still collides.

questions.verify_form: The agent deleted the template's default objects - check the tree; leaving them means building around somebody else's ground.

children.label: Build the scene
children.note: the user runs 2.1 for each object the game needs, then some of 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 depending on where the art comes from - painted in the editor, imported from a folder, or taken from an asset store. 2.5 for the level itself, which in Roblox is more of the same objects. 2.6 on every object, and 2.7 where the grid gets in the way. 2.8 when something disappears behind something else. 2.9 once per game. 2.10 as the tree fills up, and in 9v3G because a script needs the name. 2.11 whenever two objects cannot be told apart. 2.12 only in the two engines that slice a sprite sheet. 2.13 where an object has to exist more than once. 2.14 where the game needs music or an effect.

questions.question: Is there a separate object holding the level, apart from the backdrop?
questions.why: Selecting the paint option from the sprite menu allows you to custom-draw the specific platforms and obstacles needed for the level.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the creative control of hand-drawing the exact shapes and layout of the level's obstacles.
questions.check: Is there a dedicated sprite or object for the level's platforms, separate from the backdrop image?
questions.say_example: The platforms are drawn onto the backdrop itself. Put them on their own sprite or they can't collide separately.

questions.why: The dialog description confirms that a TextureRect is specifically designed to display a texture, making it the correct component for rendering a background.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose hands-on familiarity with the engine's node library and the knowledge of which specific UI controls are best suited for handling 2D assets.
questions.verify_form: The agent picked the node type that displays the background - check its description; the wrong kind will not stretch or tile the way a background needs to.
questions.check: Does the create-node dialog's description for the chosen node type say it's meant for displaying a texture/background, or something else?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the foundational understanding of how different engine-specific physics nodes dictate the built-in movement capabilities of your game objects.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose the node type for the player - check its description; the physics body meant for script-driven characters is not the same as a plain sprite.
questions.check: Does the create-node dialog's description for the chosen root node say it's meant for a script-driven character body, or something else?
questions.say_example: The player's root is a plain <Node2D>. The description for CharacterBody2D says that one's built for characters moved by script.

questions.question: Which node type should you select to display the character's image?
questions.why: Selecting the correct general-purpose sprite node from the dialog ensures the character has a visual representation in the scene.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you miss out on learning how to navigate the engine's node system to find specific visual components.
questions.verify_form: The agent chose the node that shows the character - check it; this is the one the art goes on.
questions.check: Is there a sprite/visual node on the character to display its image, matching the dialog's description for that purpose?

questions.question: Which child nodes do you need to add to make the player character function?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the hands-on understanding of how the player's physical and visual components are structured in the engine's node hierarchy.
questions.verify_form: The agent added children to the player - check that there is both a shape and something that draws it; one without the other gives an invisible or a ghostly character.

questions.question: Which basic 3D object should you create first to start building the scene?
questions.why: The context menu offers various primitive shapes like cubes and spheres, and your choice establishes the foundational building blocks for the level's geometry.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing creative control over the initial visual style and structural foundation of your game environment.
questions.verify_form: The agent created the first shape in the scene - check which primitive; everything else gets sized and placed against it.
questions.check: What primitive shape (cube, sphere, plane, etc.) was created first in the scene?

questions.verify_form: The agent picked the shape that stands in for the player - check it; the mechanics get built around whatever this is.

questions.question: Did the editor or browser tab become completely unresponsive and freeze the moment the playtest started?
questions.why: Accidentally writing an infinite loop (like a 'while' loop without a break, or a Scratch custom block without screen refresh that never exits) will lock up the engine's main thread, requiring a force-quit.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to recognize a fatal logic structure, potentially waiting indefinitely for a frozen screen or losing unsaved work when the engine has to be killed.
questions.check: Does the editor or browser tab stay responsive to input right after the playtest starts, or lock up?
